card.hook: Everything in Jackson Square points at one view: a pretty cathedral with two matching buildings beside it, red-brick rows on either side, and a general on a horse in the middle. You can barely take a bad photo here, though the crowds will test you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in Jackson Square itself, and face north across the park to St. Louis Cathedral. For a closer, lower view, walk north across the grass towards the cathedral.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the cathedral from the grass, then go 0.5x when you want the paths and greenery in the foreground. Try 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the spires and the statue.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the cathedral on the centre line, then tap it and slide darker if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning if you can, because the square can get very busy later in the day.
card.selfie_here: Head to the grass at the top of the levee in Washington Artillery Park and face the Mississippi, so Jackson Square is behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the square sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the small rise near the cannon in Washington Artillery Park and shoot back toward the square with the cathedral in view, while you pose in front of them.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is free to enter, but the cathedral and museums around it have their own visiting rules, so check their official sites before you go.
card.challenge: Get the cathedral dead centre on the gridline with a strip of lawn at the bottom and not a single shop sign in sight (tilt your phone up a touch or step sideways).
card.good_to_know: Jackson Square was once a military parade ground called the Place d'Armes. It was renamed in 1851 for Andrew Jackson, hero of the 1815 Battle of New Orleans, and his statue on horseback went up in 1856. Louisiana became US territory here in 1803, and the square became a National Historic Landmark in 1960.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in Jackson Square itself, and face north across the park to St. Louis Cathedral. For a closer, lower view, walk north across the grass towards the cathedral.

selfie_spots.why: The park sits on a levee and overlooks the river on one side and Jackson Square on the other, so turning your back to the river puts the square behind you.

card.hook: Bourbon Street at 7am is a different place: shutters down, balconies lined up, and hardly a soul in sight. Most people only see it after dark, so you'll feel like you've sneaked in early.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Bourbon Street and Iberville Street and face along Bourbon, with the subject lying to the north-east. Let the balconies and shutters line up on both sides of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural street-level view. Go to 0.5x to fit in the balconies and the full width of the street, and 2x to pick out signs and ironwork.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the building edges straight, then tap the part of the street you want clear and slide it a little darker so bright signs and neon don't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning is the quiet one: the street is nearly empty and the shutters are down. For the classic neon look, come back after dark and shoot down the strip, but expect crowds.
card.selfie_here: Try the Iberville corner early in the morning, when it's empty enough for a clear shot. For a famous street view, walk one block further down Bourbon to the St. Ann corner. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the street and balconies over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by at the Iberville corner and ask them to shoot down Bourbon Street, so you and the whole street fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your phone close and stay aware of the people around you in the evening. Do any walking-and-looking-back poses in quiet crosswalks, not in traffic, and check the day's barricade and closure status before you go.
card.challenge: Use the gridlines to get the balconies on both sides perfectly even, then see if you can spot a shuttered doorway to tuck into the corner of the frame.
card.good_to_know: Bourbon Street runs twelve blocks from Canal Street to Esplanade Avenue. Its name dates from 1721 and honours the French royal House of Bourbon, yet the look is more Spanish, thanks to the rebuilding after the Great New Orleans Fire of 1788. It has been a pedestrian mall since the early 1970s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Bourbon Street and Iberville Street and face along Bourbon, with the subject lying to the north-east. Let the balconies and shutters line up on both sides of you.

card.hook: Walk into the Louisiana Memorial Pavilion and look up. A Spitfire and a C-47 Skytrain are hanging from the ceiling, and a Higgins boat sits on the floor below. Your neck will get a workout and your camera roll will thank you.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon, in the middle of the museum complex on Andrew Higgins Drive between Camp Street and Magazine Street. There's no extra walk once you arrive. Inside, face up toward the hanging aircraft from the atrium floor. Outside, step back from a building until the whole front fits.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the atrium and the aircraft overhead. Switch to 1x for building fronts and people-sized things like the Higgins boat. Use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single aircraft or marking without moving.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep walls and windows straight, then tap the aircraft and slide to darker a touch so the bright bits don't wash out.
card.best_time: Inside, the light is much the same all day, so pick a quieter moment for clearer shots with fewer heads in them. Outside, morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the buildings.
card.selfie_here: Head to Founders Plaza, next to the life-size bronze statues of a group of WWII pilots, Anne Frank and President Franklin D. Roosevelt. Use the front camera (and 0.5x if your phone offers it) and pose beside them. Check the framing on the spot, because we can't promise the museum building fills the background.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the corner of Camp Street and Andrew Higgins Drive, where the Louisiana Memorial Pavilion is usually photographed from, while you stand in front of the pavilion.
card.rules_and_safety: The campus guide says no flash inside the galleries. Ask a member of staff about other photography rules, and check the official site for access details before you go.
card.challenge: Build a three-layer shot: aircraft overhead, an exhibit or visitor below, and the hanging planes looking tiny or huge depending on where you stand. Bonus points if nobody walks into it.
card.good_to_know: The museum began in 2000 as the National D-Day Museum, and Congress named it America's official National WWII Museum in 2003. It's in New Orleans because the Higgins boat landing craft was designed and built here. The newest pavilion, the Liberation Pavilion, opened in 2023, and the third floor has an observation deck for a closer look at the hanging aircraft.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon, in the middle of the museum complex on Andrew Higgins Drive between Camp Street and Magazine Street. There's no extra walk once you arrive. Inside, face up toward the hanging aircraft from the atrium floor. Outside, step back from a building until the whole front fits.

card.hook: Nobody leaves Café du Monde with a clean shirt, and that's half the fun. The white sugar on dark plates and clothes, set against all that green and white, makes the scene easy to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Decatur Street and St Ann Street, on the Decatur Street sidewalk, and face the café's striped awning. From there the whole café is in front of you, so you don't have to crowd the tables.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the frontage and the sign. Go to 0.5x if you want more of the street and the covered seating, and keep the phone level so the building edges stay straight. Switch to 2x for beignets and cups, rather than pushing your phone into someone's table.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the roofline and sign along the top third, then tap a bright part of the café and drag to make it a touch darker so the sugar and signs don't wash out.
card.best_time: We don't have a set best time for this one, so go when it suits you. Check your screen for glare before you shoot.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the Decatur Street sidewalk right in front of the café at 800 Decatur Street, with the green-and-white awning behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and let the café sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Jackson Square side of Decatur Street, facing the striped awning so the whole front shows, while you pose on the sidewalk in front of the café.
card.rules_and_safety: Be polite about including other guests in your shots.
card.challenge: Find the cleanest gap in the crowd and catch a close-up of a plate of beignets with a proper sugar snowfall on top.
card.good_to_know: Café du Monde began in 1862 as a simple coffee stand at the upriver end of the French Market, and the menu has changed very little since. It's known for café au lait and beignets, which are square pieces of dough with no hole under a thick coat of powdered sugar. The coffee is traditionally dark-roasted with chicory, and the orange-yellow coffee tins are a familiar sight too.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Decatur Street and St Ann Street, on the Decatur Street sidewalk, and face the café's striped awning. From there the whole café is in front of you, so you don't have to crowd the tables.

card.hook: Picture this: it's dusk, the neon flicks on, and a band starts up on the pavement while everyone crowds around. That's Frenchmen Street, and it looks good on your phone because everything is packed close together.
card.stand_here: Stand outside Dat Dog at 601 Frenchmen St and face the colourful storefront. Frenchmen Street lies to the north, about 3 minutes on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the Dat Dog front and the crowd. Go to 0.5x to fit the whole shopfront and street in one frame, or try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to catch a band across the street without stepping into their space.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest sign so the neon keeps its colour and the lights don't burn out.
card.best_time: Go at dusk or after dark, when the neon and string lights come on and the bands start playing. Hold your phone at chest height and watch for people walking through your shot.
card.selfie_here: Head to the arched entrance of the Frenchmen Art Bazaar at 619 Frenchmen St, where the vintage-style arch and hanging lights make a fun backdrop. Use the front camera, stand with the arch and lights over your shoulder, and try 0.5x if your phone has it to fit more in.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos from the street are fine, but inside clubs follow each venue's own policy. Ask before photographing musicians up close, keep any clip short, and tip if you stay. After dark, stick to the busy, well-lit blocks.
card.challenge: Can you get neon, string lights and a glowing shopfront all in one frame?
card.good_to_know: Frenchmen Street is known for its live-music clubs, and it comes alive after dark. Bands play inside and sometimes out on the pavement. The Frenchmen Art Bazaar has light-strung market stalls selling local artists' work.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand outside Dat Dog at 601 Frenchmen St and face the colourful storefront. Frenchmen Street lies to the north, about 3 minutes on foot.

card.hook: The Superdome is so big that on your first try you'll probably back up three times and still not fit it in. Don't worry, nearly everyone does it, and there's a fix.
card.stand_here: Stand on Poydras Street as you walk west from the Central Business District towards the dome. Face the stadium so its curved roofline and wall fill the frame, with the downtown office towers stacked up behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because the curved wall won't fit at 1x from close by. Then switch to 1x for a calmer shot with less stretching at the edges. If you want the office towers to look closer behind the dome, try 2x or 5x.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and keep the towers standing straight, so the curve of the dome is the only thing that bends.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light is softer than at midday. On event days crowds gather, so give yourself extra time.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the Plaza Level and stand beside the bronze Rebirth statue (Steve Gleason blocking a punt). Use the front camera at 0.5x with the dome's outer wall over your shoulder. The Tom Benson statue in Champions Square, holding the Lombardi Trophy, is another good selfie spot. I can't promise the dome will be behind you there, so check your screen before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Stand on Poydras Street walking west towards the dome and ask a passer-by to shoot you with the curved roof filling the background behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The stadium isn't open for tours, so this is an exterior shoot. A fan guide says selfie sticks are banned inside the Superdome, but it isn't an official source, so check the venue's rules before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the dome fills the frame and the towers behind it stay perfectly upright. Bonus points if you can spot the Rebirth statue on the plaza afterwards.
card.good_to_know: The Superdome opened in 1975 and is home to the New Orleans Saints. Its dome is about 207 metres across, the largest fixed domed structure in the world. It sheltered thousands of people during Hurricane Katrina in 2005, reopened in September 2006 and has hosted eight Super Bowls.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Poydras Street as you walk west from the Central Business District towards the dome. Face the stadium so its curved roofline and wall fill the frame, with the downtown office towers stacked up behind.

card.hook: Look up past the lacy iron balconies and you'll spot a little rooftop cupola sticking out above its neighbours. It's the bit of Napoleon House that says "old New Orleans" loudest.
card.stand_here: Stand on Chartres Street outside Napoleon House at 500 Chartres Street. The phone icon on the map sits right beside the building. Face along the block so the building runs down one side of your frame and the street leads off towards the church.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the street view. Tap 2x or higher if you want the church at the end of the block to look closer.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, tap the building's wall, then slide it a little darker if the sky is bright so the sky keeps some colour.
card.best_time: Early morning is likely to be quieter, with softer light along the street. Check the view when you get there, since cars and people change the scene fast.
card.selfie_here: Guides say the back courtyard of the restaurant at 500 Chartres St is the most photogenic part, so try your selfie there with the building's walls behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a little higher than your face so more of the walls fit in.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to shoot from the corner where Chartres Street meets St. Louis Street, so the corner façade and street-side walls fill the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The courtyard and interior are part of a working restaurant, so getting in may depend on being a customer. The upper floors are apartments, so keep the street as your photo spot and be considerate of diners and residents.
card.challenge: Catch a gap in the passers-by and get the cupola, the balconies and the church down the street all in one frame.
card.good_to_know: Napoleon House was built in 1794 and enlarged in 1814. A local legend says it was meant as a home for Napoleon Bonaparte after his exile, but the plan stopped when news of his death arrived in 1821. It was once the home of Nicholas Girod, a mayor of New Orleans, has been a restaurant since 1914, and became a National Historic Landmark in 1970.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Chartres Street outside Napoleon House at 500 Chartres Street. The phone icon on the map sits right beside the building. Face along the block so the building runs down one side of your frame and the street leads off towards the church.

card.hook: Half the fun of Preservation Hall happens on the street outside, with the French Quarter balconies lined up like they're waiting for the band. Start here, a minute away from the door, and you get the whole scene.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Saint Peter Street and Royal Street, by the Preservation Hall block. The hall is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot, so face north-west and look along the 700 block of Saint Peter.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full street-corner view. If the balconies are getting chopped off, tap 0.5x. Save zoom 2x for the hanging sign.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep the building edges straight, and let the balconies lead the eye to the hall.
card.best_time: Try before or after a show, when the street may be calmer. If it gets dark, use night mode and lean the phone against a wall or post to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the iron gate at 726 St. Peter Street, under the carved letters on the facade, so the entrance sits behind you. Use the front camera, and try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it to fit the lettering over your shoulder. The weathered hanging sign also makes a good backdrop, and late afternoon light suits it best.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across St. Peter Street from the hall, where they can fit the whole facade in, while you pose in front of the gate.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your phone outside during performances: photos and video aren't allowed inside, and flash is usually prohibited. Exterior photos are welcome at any time, and photos are fine before and after shows.
card.challenge: Get a shot where the balconies lead straight to the hall, with the sign peeking in and no wonky buildings.
card.good_to_know: Preservation Hall began in the 1950s as an art gallery run by Larry Borenstein, who invited local jazz musicians to play for tips. The music soon drew more attention than the paintings, and in 1961 it was renamed Preservation Hall. It now welcomes roughly 180,000 visitors a year.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Saint Peter Street and Royal Street, by the Preservation Hall block. The hall is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot, so face north-west and look along the 700 block of Saint Peter.

selfie_spots.why: A travel writer describes the carved letters on the gated entrance as the thing that makes passers-by stop, and exterior photos are described as welcome at any time, so a selfie here keeps the entrance behind you.

card.hook: Walk into Jackson Square and you'll see it straight away: a crowd of phones all pointed at the same three white spires. Guides often call this the most photographed spot in the French Quarter, and it's easy to see why.
card.stand_here: Stand in the garden area of Jackson Square, facing the front of the cathedral on the Chartres Street side. The cathedral lies to the north-west of you, and the Andrew Jackson statue sits in front of it as a handy foreground.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole facade in one frame. Go to 0.5x if you're close or want more statue and garden, and try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the spires and the clock.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then slide the brightness down a touch so the white stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Sunrise is the calmest time, and the light on the facade is soft. After dark the floodlit cathedral looks great too, while later in the day you'll probably have other people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Head to Place John Paul II, the car-free block of Chartres Street in front of the main facade, and turn so the three spires are right behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and try 0.5x if you want the whole church in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Washington Artillery Park, the park on the levee overlooking the square, while you stand on the square's lawn so the cathedral fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The cathedral is an active parish. Photos are allowed outside Mass, but flash is not.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, line the spires up with the vertical lines, and keep the statue low in the frame without letting it cut across a spire.
card.good_to_know: St. Louis Cathedral is the oldest cathedral in continuous use in the United States, a title it shares with the Royal Presidio Chapel in Monterey, California. The first church here dates from 1718, the city's founding year, and the present building dates mainly from 1850. The bell from 1819, named "Victoire", was reused and is still there.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the garden area of Jackson Square, facing the front of the cathedral on the Chartres Street side. The cathedral lies to the north-west of you, and the Andrew Jackson statue sits in front of it as a handy foreground.

card.hook: Picture a 25-foot paddlewheel turning at the back of a big white riverboat, with the French Quarter just behind you. That's the Steamboat Natchez, and she's about as New Orleans as it gets.
card.stand_here: Stand on the riverfront promenade in Woldenberg Riverfront Park, near where the steamboat docks. Face the river: the Natchez is just to the south-east, with the Mississippi and the Crescent City Connection bridge behind her.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the whole boat, the river and the bridge in one shot. Then try 1x for a tidier, more natural look. Go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the calliope, the pipes and the wheel.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the boat, then slide the brightness a little darker so the white upper decks and the sky don't wash out.
card.best_time: Whenever the boat is in port. Cruise times change, so check the official site before you head over.
card.selfie_here: Try the grass strip by the river bank in Woldenberg Riverfront Park, where the boat is moored. Use the front camera, turn your back to the water so the Natchez sits over your shoulder, and try 0.5x to squeeze her in.
card.rules_and_safety: The riverfront promenade is an outdoor public park, but it's being rebuilt, so check for closures. Going on board is a separate matter, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Turn on your gridlines, keep the horizon dead level, and get the whole boat on the lower third with the bridge floating behind her.
card.good_to_know: The Natchez was built in 1975 and is about 265 feet (81 m) long. Her wheel is white oak and steel, and her steam calliope can play 32 notes. A fire broke out on board in 2022, and she returned to service in 2023.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the riverfront promenade in Woldenberg Riverfront Park, near where the steamboat docks. Face the river: the Natchez is just to the south-east, with the Mississippi and the Crescent City Connection bridge behind her.

card.hook: Here's the surprise: you don't have to get inside to get the shot. The worn white plaster wall on Basin Street has rows of old tombs peeking over the top, and that's already a proper spooky-pretty scene.
card.stand_here: Stand on Basin Street, along the cemetery's outer wall just before the entrance. Walk north-west along Basin Street to get there, then turn to face the wall.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the long run of wall and the street. Go to 1x for the plaster and the gate, then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the tomb rows above the wall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the top of the wall up with a horizontal line so the tombs sit neatly above it.
card.best_time: Pick a quieter time on the pavement so it's easier to step back for a wide shot. If you can, tap the wall and drag the brighter/darker slider a little darker so the plaster keeps its texture.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt the phone up a touch so the landmark fits over your shoulder. Hold your phone close to your body while you line it up.
card.rules_and_safety: Going inside normally means a guided tour, so check the official site first. Photography is allowed on the official tours, but don't touch, lean on or sit on the tombs, and don't leave offerings. Paths inside are narrow and uneven, so wear sturdy shoes. Out on Basin Street, stay on the pavement while you wait for traffic to clear.
card.challenge: Keep the phone level and get the top of the wall on a gridline with the tomb rows sitting right above it. Bonus points if you pull it off without any wonky, tilted walls.
card.good_to_know: St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 opened in 1789, after a fire in 1788 led to the city being redesigned. It covers just one square block, yet many thousands of people are buried here, mostly in above-ground tombs. Marie Laveau is believed to lie in the Glapion family tomb, and Homer Plessy of the Plessy v. Ferguson case is buried here too.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Basin Street, along the cemetery's outer wall just before the entrance. Walk north-west along Basin Street to get there, then turn to face the wall.

rules.rule: Photography is allowed on the official guided tours, but touching the tombs is not.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific spot inside St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 where a visitor should stand with the cemetery behind them, so selfie_spots is empty rather than guessed. Marie Laveau's tomb is named as a popular photo subject, but no page says where to stand to photograph a visitor with it, and visitors must not mark it. The cemetery is closed to independent entry, so any photo spot is reachable only on a licensed tour; the guide-photo offer is the only photo-taking help a page mentions, and it names no location, so ask_someone_spot is null. No page states any rule about selfie sticks; the two that mention them (Bourbon Legends Tour and GenealogyBank) only call them helpful. One blog places a cemetery across from Commander's Palace, which is Lafayette Cemetery No. 1, not this site, so it was excluded. The coordinates given were not checked against any page.

card.hook: Here's the fun part: you can get a great Lafayette Cemetery photo without going in. A white wall of sealed vaults, an iron gate, and oak trees leaning over the tomb roofs all fit in one frame from the street.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Washington Avenue and Prytania Street, on the sidewalk across from the cemetery's white wall, just outside the main gate. Face the gate so the wall of vaults runs along one side and the tomb tops and oaks rise behind the iron fence.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the gate and the wall. Switch to 0.5x to fit the whole corner and the trees above it. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the tomb tops and urns peeking over the wall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the white wall up with a horizontal line so it doesn't slope, then tap the wall and slide it a little darker so it doesn't glare against the dark trees.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late afternoon light is kind to the white wall. It's also usually calmer then, before the tour groups gather at the gate.
card.selfie_here: Try the iron front gate on Washington Avenue, where you can see the rows of tombs through the bars. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the gate and tombs sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sidewalk across Washington Avenue from the cemetery entrance (across from Commander's Palace) while you pose by the gate, so they can frame you with the gate and tombs behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Access has changed over the years, so check the official site before you go. Stay on the public pavement, because the city says all tombs and graves are private property and trespassing isn't allowed. The city has also called the cemetery an unsafe environment for general visitation, and drones should stay at home.
card.challenge: Spot the urns on top of the tombs, zoom in until they fill the frame, and see if you can keep the white wall perfectly straight.
card.good_to_know: Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 was founded in 1833 and was New Orleans' first planned cemetery. It fills a single city block and holds roughly 1,100 family tombs and about 7,000 people. The cross-shaped layout was designed so funeral processions could move through, and the cemetery has appeared in a long list of films and TV shows.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Washington Avenue and Prytania Street, on the sidewalk across from the cemetery's white wall, just outside the main gate. Face the gate so the wall of vaults runs along one side and the tomb tops and oaks rise behind the iron fence.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found states a selfie-stick or tripod rule for Lafayette No. 1, so the rules list is empty. The page that mentions tripods (Crescent City Tours) names Jackson Square, City Park and some plantations, not this cemetery. Status is conflicting: Airial and ShutterCoach describe it as closed, while 2026 news (Fox 8, Yahoo) says it was to reopen for guided tours on October 1 (9 a.m. to 1 p.m., groups of up to 16). The city's Division of Cemeteries page lists it as open only through guided tours. The outside-the-gate photos are the only public-facing options. The city's filming guide says drones are not permitted in city-owned cemeteries; this is not a selfie or tripod rule, so I left it out of rules. None of the pages gives a precise selfie position, so both selfie spots are inferred from gate and wall descriptions. The Prytania Street wall spot is weak. The ask-someone spot comes from an address note, not a photo-spot recommendation. The Pondering Padawan blog shows a selfie taken in the cemetery but names no location, so I did not use it.

card.hook: Picture three grand buildings standing shoulder to shoulder, all staring at the same leafy square. The Cabildo is the one on the left, and it has survived two big fires.
card.stand_here: Stand in Jackson Square, on the Chartres Street side, and face the buildings. The Cabildo lies to the west, about 1 minute on foot, with St. Louis Cathedral to its right and the Presbytère beyond that.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the Cabildo, the cathedral and the Presbytère all in one frame. Try 0.5x if you're close and want more of the square's fence and trees. Then zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the eagle on the roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the building edges up with the vertical lines so those tall facades stay straight.
card.best_time: Sunrise is the one to aim for. The square is emptier and the light is soft on the cathedral facade.
card.selfie_here: Try Pirates Alley, the little corridor between the Cabildo and St. Louis Cathedral. From the front of the Cabildo, look to the right of the building to find it. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the buildings over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand in Jackson Square in front of the Cabildo, with the square's central area in view, while you pose with the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the building from the square, but museum entry and any interior access may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Walk about a minute towards the building and zoom in to catch the American eagle on the pediment, then show it off to your friends.
card.good_to_know: The Cabildo was built as the seat of Spanish colonial city government and is now part of the Louisiana State Museum. The Louisiana Purchase transfer ceremonies took place here in 1803. A fire in 1988 destroyed the cupola and the whole third floor, and the building reopened in 1994.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Jackson Square, on the Chartres Street side, and face the buildings. The Cabildo lies to the west, about 1 minute on foot, with St. Louis Cathedral to its right and the Presbytère beyond that.

card.hook: Along the Mississippi riverfront, one building has a giant glass cylinder sticking out of it, and you can't miss it. It's the Amazon exhibit, and with water and sky behind it, it makes a very easy photo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Woldenberg Park outside the Audubon Aquarium of the Americas, at the edge of the French Quarter off Canal Street, and face the building. Step back until the glass cylinder and the front of the building fit together with the river or sky behind them.
card.zoom: Zoom 1x works for most shots. Switch to zoom 0.5x from the park to fit the whole building and the cylinder in, and use zoom 2x or more inside to pick out a single tank, a turtle or a ray.
card.make_it_pop: Inside, tap the fish or animal you want, then slide the brightness down a touch to make it darker so the bright tank water doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Outside, soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder than harsh midday sun. Inside, the tanks look the same at any hour, but a quieter time makes clear shots easier.
card.selfie_here: Head to the plaza in front of the aquarium, beside the 90-foot linear water feature (it's open during aquarium hours, weather permitting). Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and hold it a bit high, so the aquarium building should sit over your shoulder, since the feature is set right in front of it.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo at the Goldring Woldenberg Riverfront Park sign by the aquarium plaza, with you by the sign and the aquarium building in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is permitted throughout the aquarium. Guides disagree on flash, so skip it near the exhibits. Check the official site before you go for entry details and any photography rules.
card.challenge: Walk through the Caribbean reef tunnel and catch a fish arching overhead. Take a few shots, or use Live Photos, and pick the best one afterwards.
card.good_to_know: The aquarium first opened on 1 September 1990 and focuses on aquatic life of the Americas. It reopened on 8 June 2023 after a $41 million renovation that brought the Audubon Insectarium into the same building. Of its roughly 10,000 animals, look out for the white alligator in the Mississippi River gallery.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Woldenberg Park outside the Audubon Aquarium of the Americas, at the edge of the French Quarter off Canal Street, and face the building. Step back until the glass cylinder and the front of the building fit together with the river or sky behind them.

card.hook: Picture a wide open square, one big oak tree and a grand auditorium standing behind it. On a weekend there might be drumming too. That's Congo Square, and it's very easy to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand in Congo Square, the open ground in front of the Municipal Auditorium, and face the auditorium with the big oak tree in your frame. The wider park lies to the north-east of this spot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the square, the oak and the auditorium together. Go to 0.5x for more open ground and sky. For the statues or a performer, try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) and keep a polite distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the oak tree on one third of the frame with the auditorium behind it, and keep the horizon level.
card.best_time: Go when the square isn't too busy if you want clear shots of the ground and the tree. If you want the drumming and the buzz, go at a weekend and expect people in your pictures. The park entrance arch is lit up along Rampart Street in the evening.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the granite-tile plaza in Congo Square, beside the oak tree, with the Municipal Auditorium behind you. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if your phone has it, so the tree and building both squeeze in over your shoulder. For a second one, stand just inside the lit arched entrance on North Rampart Street, with the arch behind you, facing back toward the street.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the corner of North Rampart and Dumaine streets with the whole park behind you, and ask a passer-by to take your photo facing you with the park in view.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is usually fine for a normal park visit. If you're using professional gear for commercial work or going to a ticketed event, clear it with park management first. The park is fenced, so check the official site before you go for current access and any event restrictions.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice: once with the weekend crowd and performers, and once without. Which one tells the better story?
card.good_to_know: Louis Armstrong Park covers 32 acres in the Tremé neighbourhood, just across Rampart Street from the French Quarter. It's named after New Orleans-born jazz legend Louis Armstrong, and you'll find a 12-foot statue of him by Elizabeth Catlett inside. The park hosted the first New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival in 1970, and Congo Square is known for its role in the history of African American music and spiritual practice.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Congo Square, the open ground in front of the Municipal Auditorium, and face the auditorium with the big oak tree in your frame. The wider park lies to the north-east of this spot.

No page I found mentions selfie sticks or tripods, or a safety point, so those fields are empty. Lonely Planet names a Louis Armstrong statue and a Sidney Bechet bust inside the park, but no page I found recommends them as a photo spot, so I left them out.

card.hook: Picture a whole block of iron balconies, painted fronts and shop windows all marching away from you in one neat line. The corner of Royal and Dumaine gives you exactly that, and it's often a little quieter than the busier St. Peter Street corner.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement at the corner of Royal Street and Dumaine Street, by the corner balcony. Face north up Royal Street so the shops and colourful building fronts run away from you along the block.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the balconies. If the pavement is too narrow to fit the whole facade, tap 0.5x. Try 2x when you want to pick out a single balcony or shopfront.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the buildings upright, then put a balcony in the top corner of the frame and let the street lead the eye into the distance.
card.best_time: Early morning tends to give you emptier balconies. The street is busy through the day, so be patient, wait for a gap in the people, then shoot.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the corner of Royal and Dumaine, on the corner balcony. It's a blogger's favourite and a quieter alternative when the famous St. Peter corner is crowded. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the balcony over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Along the balcony stretch around the 200-300 block of Royal, ask a passer-by to frame you with the iron balconies and the street running behind you, ideally in late afternoon.
card.rules_and_safety: The balconies belong to private buildings, so take your photos from the public pavement and keep it clear for others. Stay aware of your surroundings, keep your phone out of sight between shots, and avoid poorly lit blocks in the far reaches of the Quarter before dawn.
card.challenge: Get one frame with a balcony in the top corner and not a single stranger in the street. You'll have to wait for your moment, so call it a test of patience.
card.good_to_know: Royal Street is one of the original streets of the French Quarter, dating from the early 18th century. Today it's known for antique shops, art galleries and hotels. It starts at Canal Street, and the upper part towards Canal Street is the one best known for antiques.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement at the corner of Royal Street and Dumaine Street, by the corner balcony. Face north up Royal Street so the shops and colourful building fronts run away from you along the block.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found states rules about selfie sticks or tripods on Royal Street, so the rules list is empty. Timing advice is consistent across sources: early morning gives emptier balconies, and <cite index="8-6">Royal Street is pedestrian-only on weekends after noon</cite> according to one guide, which I did not verify. The ask-someone spot is taken from a bike-tour blog's group-photo advice rather than a dedicated photography guide, and the blog's own spot is for a group shot, so a single visitor is an adaptation. I did not confirm the given coordinates (29.95960, -90.06330) against any page, and the sources are blogs of varying age, so check the corners on a map before going.
